analysis: All four changed files are test-only: SSDHybridCheckpointCoordinationTests, SSDHybridCheckpointRecencyTests, SSDOwnedEntryRetirementTests and SSDShorterCheckpointRestoreTests. No production code is in this batch, so there is no new attack surface or weakened control. I did not see the production SSD cache changes the tests describe: shared reader leases on the same file, a recency refresh rate-limited by recencyRefreshSeconds (60), TTL retirement with the new unusedSince cutoff, and whole-root maintenance that keeps a file whose in-memory hit is newer than its mtime. Those would sit under T-041 (SSD prefix cache, 30-minute sliding TTL). What the tests assert is consistent with the T-041 posture. A sweep one TTL after the last persisted hit removes the file (RecencyTests lines 174-175). An unconditional retirement path remains when no cutoff is given (RetirementTests lines 63-66). A corrupt file is deleted only by a sole reader (CoordinationTests, corruptFileRemovedBySoleReader). Epoch, ciphertext and KEK handling are unchanged, and the tests check the epoch is not rotated by per-file removal. One point for the production review: the tests show a hit can keep a file alive past the persisted mtime plus TTL, up to 801 s past the persisted hit in the test. Whole-root maintenance seems to read the in-memory index recency and write that time back to the mtime. That could keep the effective TTL slightly above the 1800 s sliding bound, depending on the refresh interval. Whether the production change enforces the T-041 30-minute cap against the true last hit (not a rate-limited mtime), and whether the mtime write-back is no-follow and root-confined (setAttributesIfSafe is used), needs checking in the non-test source, which was not supplied. The SSDShorterCheckpointRestoreTests patch excerpt is truncated and its unit text was not supplied; it only changes gating in a same-ID replacement test.
